קושי' הגמרא במקומו ואם כן הך דינא דר"נ דמברחת לא קנה מקבל במחלוקת תנאים שנוי' דלר"ש לא קנה אבל לחכמים קושי' הגמרא במקומו וקנהו מקבל וקושי' תוס' שפיר איך קרשיב ר"נ מברחת בכלל חמשה דלא קנה דהא פלוגתא דתנאי היא וא"ש וע"ז תי' התוס' דהיכי דאיכא גילוי דעת משום אנסובי לכולא עלמא לא קנה המקב' והיינו כמ"ש דאף ר"ת מודה בזה דלא שייך הואיל ולא קנהו בעל יקנה לוקח דהא אין רצונם כלל. והדברים ברורים ומוכרחים. ולפ"ז יפה כתב הרמ"א אם נראה לב"ד שלא כיון לערמה רק למתנה אין הפיר' בפי' למתנה דזהו פשיטא רק שלא גילה דעתו להדיא דהוא רק לערמ' אם כן היינו דנתכוון למתנה גמורה דאנן סהדי דיותר ניחא ליה במקבל מן ב"ח ואי לא יקנה הוא יקנה ב"ח ואם כן אנן סהדי דלמתנה נתכוון וזהו אמרו של רמ"א אע"ג דנתכוון להברחה רק מה בכך מ"מ קנה המקבל מתנה כדינו של ר"ת וזהו ברור. אך מזה נראה דכל טיב דינו של הברחה הוא ביש נכסים ברשות מקבל אבל אם לא יצאו מרשות הנותן לכולא עלמא אין בו ממש והוא ערמה והברחה גמורה בכל אופן דאם לא כן הוה ליה לרמ"א להזכיר דעת הרא"ש ומהר"ם החולקים ומצי הנותן המוחזק לומר קים ליה כוותיה אלא דלא יתכן רק בישנו ביד המקבל ואם כן מי יוציא מידו נגד ר"ת והנך רבוותא דלעיל והנה הרב הב"ח דעתו גם כן דבישנו הנכסים ביד הנותן אפילו בנותן מקצת מ"מ הוי הברחה דחזינן הערמה דהא נכסים ברשותו והש"ך כתב דדינו צ"ע. ובאמת יש לפקפק דהא הרא"ש מדמה הך אומדנא לאומדנא דמתנת ש"מ דקיימא לן חוזר ובמקצת הא קיימא לן דאינו חוזר אף דנכסים ברשות הש"מ ולא נימא אלו רצונו ליתנם למקבל בהחלט הוה ליה ליתנו לרשותו. ולא להחזיקו תחת ידו ודוחק לחלק. וגם מדברי תשובת הר"ם מרדכי פ' גט פשוט בא' שקנה קרקעות והעלה שטר מכירה בשם קרובים להפקיע כתובת אשה ופסק הר"ם דהוי רק הברחה ואשה גובה כתובה אף כפי הנראה בתשובה שייר לעצמו ואם כן למה דן בי' הר"ם דין מברח' ש"מ לכאורה כהב"ח דהואיל נכסים בחזקת הבעל בכ"מ הוי הברחה אך אם כן הא דנתן הר"ם הטעם דאל"כ לא הנחת לאשה שתגבה כתובה כי תמיד ימצא גואלים שיקנה מטלטלין ויתן להם כי מובטח להם שלא יעכבם לעצמו הא כשהם ביד קרובים עדיין לא הוי הברחה דהא הוא רק במקצת ועדיין לא מצא מהר"ם תרופה לחשש הלזה ועכצ"ל דהיכי דאיכא אומדנא דמוכח וידי' מוכיחות אפילו במקצת ואפילו הם בבית קרובים מ"מ דנין ביה דין הברחה. וכדאמרינן בגמרא היכי דגלי' דעתיה גשום אנסובי לכ"ע הוי הברחה וע"ש בתוס' ד"ה אפילו וכו' דבכהאי גונא אפילו במקצת דנין ביה דין הברחה ע"ש ובאופן זה היה נדון של מהר"ם ולכך לא נחית לחלק בין מתנה במקצת לכולו ולכן אין כאן ראיה ברורה לדברי הב"ח גם מה שכתב דאף ר"ת מודה היכי דישט ביד הנותן כו' לכולא עלמא לא קנהו המקבל וטורפן אף דמתשובת הרא"ש כלל ע"ח משמע כן לכאורה מכל מקום אין ראיה דעובדא דרא"ש היה הברחה ניכרת כמו שהאריך בתשובה:

ואין לנו לחדש סברות בלי ראי' מוכרחת ועי' תשוב' רמ"א סי' ס"ז דעמד מהרש"ל במ"ש מרדכי דגובה הוא ממקבל מתנה דהא לדעת ר"ת זוכה מקבל מתנה והגיה מהרש"ל דיש למחוק מילת הוא רק גובה מקבל מתנה והרמ"א כתב כי אינו מבין הגהתו מה גבי' שייך במקבל מתנה הלא כבר היא תחת ידו ולכך חשב להגיה באופן אחר ובמרדכי שלפנינו מוגה כהגהת מהרש"ל וצ"ל דס"ל למהרש"ל דעובדא שם לא היה מקבל מתנה מוחזק בנכסים כלל רק בא לגבות בשטרו לכך אמר דגובה בשטרו ואתי שפיר לישנא דגובה וזה מבואר דלא כב"ח דאף בכהאי גונא אמרה ר"ת ולכן דינו צריך לעיון:
en_segments: Even land, etc. The Shach asks: granted that in an actual sale or gift the recipient becomes owner, but where the transfer was only a device to hide assets from creditors, the recipient should owe the property back to the transferor. The transferor's creditor should then collect it through the rule of Rabbi Natan. Why is a special doctrine of fraudulent transfer necessary? This objection should not be directed to the responsum of the Rosh from which the ruling derives. The Rosh himself says that the creditor possesses the standard lien on movable property together with land, so by strict law he could collect from the gift recipient, and only the market-protection enactment would ordinarily shield the recipient. In a fraudulent transfer that enactment does not apply. Why did the Rosh need this entire framework? If a fraudulent transfer is automatically void, the creditor should collect even without any such lien. One answer is that the Rosh meant his ruling to apply even according to Rabbenu Tam and those who agree with him, who hold in Ketubot, chapter HaIshah Shenaflu, that a sham transfer designed to hide property from creditors can nevertheless vest title in the recipient. Even Rabbenu Tam may agree that in the Rosh's case the ordinary market-protection enactment does not shield the recipient. More likely, the Rosh's particular case involved uncertainty whether the transfer was truly fraudulent or was a genuine gift. Because the recipient held the property, that doubt by itself would prevent extraction. The Rosh therefore reasoned that under strict Torah lien law the creditor would collect from the recipient, so the recipient's only defense is the rabbinic market-protection enactment. A doubt concerning the scope of a rabbinic enactment is judged according to the underlying law. The creditor can therefore recover. This also explains why the Tur copied two responsa of the Rosh consecutively concerning fraudulent transfers. The Derishah asks why both are needed. In one case the fraudulent intent was clearly established, so the Rosh ruled that even an oral creditor could recover from the recipient. In the second case the intent was uncertain, so ordinary doubt would favor the possessor. The creditor could recover only because he had a formal movable-property-with-land lien under the underlying law and the market-protection enactment was not extended to a doubtful fraudulent transaction. The two responsa therefore address different situations. Accordingly, the Shach's question is answered with respect to the Rosh's responsum. The creditor cannot recover the fruits merely because the transaction might have been a sham, since the fraudulent character itself is uncertain. Strict lien law did not reach those fruits through the ordinary clause, as the Rosh explains, and the burden of proof remains upon the one seeking to remove them from the recipient. The Mechaber, however, states broadly that even an oral creditor can recover from the recipient, implying a case where the transfer is clearly known to be fraudulent. The Shach's question therefore remains against the Mechaber unless we clarify the recipient's rights to the fruits of a sham transfer. That issue itself requires examination. The Rosh, in the chapter HaIshah Shenaflu, writes concerning a woman's sham transfer that the recipient eats the fruits. The Mechaber in Even HaEzer, siman 90, seif 7, appears to rule likewise. The Rosh gives two reasons. First, the woman intended to prevent her husband from benefiting. If the fruits remained hers, they would belong to the husband, defeating her purpose. Second, there is a strong presumption that she intended the recipient to enjoy the fruits, because otherwise no one would agree to exert effort cultivating and guarding property for nothing. These reasons lead to different results with an ordinary creditor. The first is specific to a wife and husband. It reflects Rabbenu Tam and Rabbenu Shimshon's reasoning that if the recipient does not acquire, the husband will, while the woman clearly prefers the recipient. Yet the Rosh generally disagrees with that reasoning regarding the corpus of a sham transfer. He explains that the transferor may simply be mistaken, thinking that neither recipient nor husband or creditor will acquire. Once informed that the scheme fails, he may prefer his own legal counterparty over the recipient. Why then does the Rosh use the first rationale for fruits? The answer appears to be that the Rosh limits the transferor's mistake to the corpus, where the transferor may have imagined a special device preventing both sides from acquiring. With fruits, however, there is no corresponding necessity to assume such a legal mistake. If the fruits do not go to the recipient, they necessarily go to the husband under ordinary marital law. The woman's purpose therefore indicates that she preferred the recipient with respect to fruits. In that respect the Rosh can agree with Rabbenu Tam. However. This first rationale is specific to a wife, where the category of property unknown to the husband may support her expectation. With an ordinary creditor, the Rosh necessarily says that the transferor was mistaken even about the corpus, because no analogous category exists. The creditor can therefore take the corpus. The same mistake can extend to the fruits, and one cannot infer from the wife's case that the recipient permanently acquires them against an ordinary creditor. The second rationale, compensation for the recipient's labor, could apply equally to an ordinary creditor. Why would a recipient cultivate and guard the transferor's property without benefit? At first glance this suggests that even in a creditor case the fruits should belong to the recipient. Yet later in that same discussion the Rosh explicitly says that once the transferor learns the scheme is ineffective and that the creditor can seize the property, the transferor prefers to keep the fruits himself until actual foreclosure rather than enrich the gift recipient. That statement seems to contradict the second rationale if the latter were independently decisive. The reconciliation is that before discovery of the scheme, while the transferor believes the sham transfer successfully blocks the creditor, he intends the recipient to enjoy the fruits as compensation for managing the property. After the fraud is uncovered and the property is exposed to immediate foreclosure, the reason for giving away future fruits disappears. The transferor can manage the property himself until foreclosure and has no reason to continue compensating the recipient for a device that no longer works. Thus, where the Mechaber discusses fruits already consumed by the recipient before the fraudulent nature of the transfer was established, those fruits can indeed belong to the recipient outright. This also accords with the Ran, who writes that the recipient acquires fruits because the transferor effectively waives them. Although the Ran follows Rabbenu Tam regarding the principal transfer, his reasoning about fruits can apply more broadly. The Mechaber's ruling is therefore correct, though not for the reason assumed by the Shach.

As an absolute gift, etc. Although his intention was to hide the property from creditors, the wording at first appears self-contradictory. If he intended an absolute gift, how can we say his intention was merely concealment? And if he intended only concealment, how can it be called an absolute gift? The Rashba and Ramban responsa that serve as the source do not use this formulation. Moreover, if the donor plainly intended an actual gift, its validity would be obvious and the Rama would teach nothing. It appears that the Rama rules like Rabbenu Tam, who holds that a document of concealment can nevertheless vest title in the recipient. The Gemara's logic is that if the recipient does not acquire, the creditor will, and since the donor clearly prefers the recipient to the creditor, we infer a real gift. Maharam and the Rosh disagree, and the Rosh reports that leading authorities sided with Maharam. Maharik likewise follows them. But Rabbenu Tam, Tosafot, and Rabbenu Shimshon support the recipient, and the Rashba, as the Beit Yosef reports in a responsum, agreed that one who relies on that view has support. Raah, Ritva, Ran, and Rivash, siman 142, likewise rule that way. Where the recipient is already in possession, who can remove the property against so many authorities? This also appears to be the Darkei Moshe's understanding. He cites many authorities who agree with Rabbenu Tam that a gift made to avoid a creditor can be acquired by the recipient and does not mention a contrary view. His gloss here is therefore directed to Rabbenu Tam. Rabbenu Tam did not mean that every transfer survives even where there is conclusive proof that the donor never intended the recipient to acquire. Where a clear and specific circumstance demonstrates that no gift was intended, everyone agrees that the recipient acquires nothing. We cannot invent a gift solely because otherwise the creditor would acquire property that the donor did not want him to receive, where an unmistakable factual presumption establishes that the donor never intended to give the property away. The Rosh's responsa and Maharik support this limitation. Tosafot in the chapter HaIshah Shenaflu prove the same point. According to Rashi's explanation of the concealment case, the woman expressly told the witnesses that her sole intention was to hide the assets. Tosafot ask why Rav Anan and Rava, who disagree with Rav Nachman, would nevertheless hold that the recipient acquires. If Tosafot adopted Rabbenu Tam without limitation, there would be no question: even an intentionally concealed transfer should vest title because otherwise the husband would acquire. The Gemara's answer that Rabbi Shimon treats the property like assets unknown to the husband would matter only according to Rabbi Shimon, whereas the other authorities could follow the Sages. Tosafot's question therefore assumes that when the evidence clearly establishes that the woman intended no gift at all, even Rabbenu Tam agrees the recipient cannot acquire. The inference that the donor prefers the recipient over the creditor cannot overcome an express manifestation of contrary intent. This also clarifies Tosafot in Bava Batra 150b, in the passage beginning "and these are," where they ask how Rav Nachman can count a concealed transfer among five cases in which a transfer of all property is ineffective, since he does not ordinarily list matters dependent on dispute. Maharshal and Maharsha struggled to identify the dispute. Maharsha says it is merely the dispute of Rav Anan and Rava against Rav Nachman, but that is difficult. Amoraim regularly state their own rulings even when other amoraim disagree. "Do you challenge one person from another?" If a sage could not state a halachic position because a colleague disputed him, very little law could ever be taught. Rather, Tosafot follow Rabbenu Tam. The Gemara asks that if the recipient does not acquire, the husband should acquire, and answers that Rabbi Shimon treats the assets like property unknown to the husband. According to the Sages, however, even unknown assets are acquired by the husband. The original difficulty would remain, and the recipient would have to acquire. Thus the validity of a concealment transfer depends upon the Tannaitic dispute between Rabbi Shimon and the Sages. Tosafot therefore properly ask how Rav Nachman could list concealment among the five undisputed cases. Tosafot answer that where there is an explicit disclosure that the transfer was made only because she was about to marry, everyone agrees the recipient does not acquire. That is exactly the limitation stated above. Even Rabbenu Tam agrees that where the donor's intention not to make a gift is conclusively revealed, the recipient cannot acquire merely because the alternative is that the husband or creditor acquires. The point is clear and compelling. The Rama's phrase can now be read precisely. "If it appears to beit din that he did not intend mere artifice but an actual gift" does not mean that he explicitly announced an unconditional gift, which would be obvious. It means that he did not expressly reveal an intention that the transfer be only a sham. In such a case we infer an actual gift because we know that he prefers the recipient to the creditor. Thus, even though his motive was to hide the property, the recipient acquires under Rabbenu Tam's rule. That is the Rama's novelty. This suggests that the rule is strongest where the property has actually entered the recipient's possession. If it never left the donor's possession, the transaction may be treated by everyone as a pure device. Otherwise the Rama should have noted the contrary positions of the Rosh and Maharam, since the donor who remains in possession could invoke kim li in their favor. When the recipient is the possessor, however, the numerous authorities supporting Rabbenu Tam prevent removal from him. The Bach likewise holds that where the property remains in the donor's possession, even a transfer of only part of the property can be treated as concealment because the circumstances reveal the artifice. The Shach leaves that ruling in doubt. There is reason to question the Bach. The Rosh compares the presumption governing a concealment gift to that governing a gift by a person on his deathbed. A gift of all property by a person on his deathbed is revocable, but a gift of only part is not, even though the property may physically remain in the donor's possession. We do not say that if he truly intended an absolute gift he would have placed it immediately in the recipient's hands. It is therefore difficult to make possession alone decisive. Maharam's responsum cited by Mordechai in the chapter Get Pashut also requires analysis. A man purchased land and caused the deed to be written in the names of relatives in order to defeat his wife's ketubah. Maharam ruled that it was only a concealment device and that the wife could collect. The facts appear to indicate that the husband retained some property. If so, one might infer like the Bach that because the property effectively remained under the husband's control, even a partial transfer was treated as concealment. But Maharam explains his concern differently: otherwise no woman could reliably collect a ketubah, because every husband could find relatives to hold nominal title while trusting that they would not keep the assets for themselves. If a partial transfer to relatives were never concealment, Maharam's solution would not address that danger. The correct inference is that where there is a clear factual presumption demonstrating fraudulent purpose, even a partial transfer and even property physically held by relatives can be treated as concealment. The Gemara likewise says that where the woman expressly reveals that the transfer is because of impending marriage, everyone treats it as concealment, and Tosafot indicate that this can apply even to a partial transfer. Maharam's case involved that kind of clear evidence. He therefore had no need to distinguish between a transfer of all property and part of it. It does not provide a general proof for the Bach's broader rule. Likewise, the Bach's claim that Rabbenu Tam himself agrees that whenever the property remains with the donor the recipient acquires nothing is not conclusively established. A responsum of the Rosh, rule 78, may at first appear to support it, but that case involved clearly proven concealment and therefore does not decide the broader question. And we should not invent new distinctions without compelling proof. See the Rama's responsum, siman 67, discussing Maharshal's correction of Mordechai. Mordechai's text said that "he collects from the gift recipient." Maharshal objected that according to Rabbenu Tam the gift recipient acquires, and proposed deleting a word so that the text instead means that the gift recipient himself collects. The Rama says he does not understand the correction: what "collection" is needed if the recipient already possesses the property? He therefore proposed a different emendation. Our printed Mordechai follows Maharshal's correction. Maharshal must have understood that in Mordechai's case the gift recipient was not physically in possession but merely came to collect under his document. In that setting it is meaningful to say that he "collects." This shows that Maharshal understood Rabbenu Tam's rule to apply even where the recipient was not already holding the property, contrary to the Bach's categorical distinction. The matter therefore requires study.

he_segments: אם יש לו מעות וכו' וכ' הש"ך ס"ק א' דה"ה לענין כתובת אשה אם יש ליתומים מעות בעין כפי מה שכתב הטור א"ע סי' ק' וכן הוא בתשובה מהרשד"ם בשם מהו' דוד כהן סי' קמ"ג לח"מ ומה דפשיטא לי' לדידי מספקא טובי חדא דהא מבואר לקמן בסי' ק"ז דאם יש ליתומים מטלטלין וקרקעות א"י לומר תן לי מטלטלין ועיי' בב"י מ"ש בשם רבינו יונה דה"ה מעות וקרקע ואם כן כיון דיכול לדחותו מן מעות למקרקעי איך לא יכול לדחותו מן מעות למטלטלין הלא תמי' יפה כח מטלטלין מן קרקע ומקרי מיטב ועדי' נגד קרקע ובטו' א"ע חפשתי ולא מצאתי דבר כלל ובתשובת רשד"ם הוא טעות דכתב כן דכתב הר"ב דכ"ץ ומזה העתיק הש"ך ר"ד כהן ואינו כי לא כתב מעולם על ר"ד כ"ץ רק הוא הרשב"ץ וכן הוא להדיא ברשד"ם חלק א"ע סי' קל"א כפי מה שמצאתי בתשובה לרבינו שמעון בר צמח שאם הניח הבעל מעות בעין האשה גובה כתובה ותוספ' ונדוניא ממעות ואם כן צא ולמד בתשוב' רשב"ץ ח"ג סי' צ"ט דף כ"ה שכתב בפשיטות באלמנה שרוצה לגבות מעות מיתומים והם רוצים ליתן לה קרקע הואיל היא הקרקע שהכניסה לבעלה ופסק דהואיל דהיא הקרקע שהכניסה אין בידה לתבוע מעות עכ"ל הרי דלולי דהכניסה הך קרקע צריך לפרוע לה מן מעות וזה נגד כל הפוסקים הנ"ל. וצריך לומר דכל הכתובה בימי הרשב"ץ היה נהוגים לכתוב ביה מטלטלין וקרקע ואם כן מדינא משתעבדי מטלטלין דיתמי ולא מתקנת הגאונים כמבואר לקמן סי' ק"ז ע"ש ואם כן אזלא הטעמים מ"ש המחברים דלכך לא מצי לתבוע מעות או מטלטלין דהם לא משתעבדו רק מכח תקנת הגאונים וקרקע משתעבד ד"ת כי בנדון זה אף מטלטלין משתעבדים ד"ת. ואם כן אף הנ"ל א"ש דיש לה מעות וא"י לדחות לקרקע אבל בכתובה דלא כתב הכי דדינא לדחותו ממעות לקרקע נראה דכ"ש דיכול לדחותו למטלטלין דמיקרי מיטב. ובאמת עם כל זה אני מפקפק דכל דינו וטעמו של ר"ת דצריך ליתן מעות למלוה הוא מטעם דזוזי יהיב זוזי שקיל ואף בזה נחלק עליו רבינו חיים הכהן ואם כן הנ"מ בנדוני' שהכניסה לבעלה אבל כתובה הא לא יהבי זוזי כלל אלא שבזה בטלה דעתי נגד דעת הרשב"ץ. אבל ברור דלא מיירי רק במקום שכותבין מטלטלין וקרקע כמו שהוכחתי מדברים הנ"ל אבל במקום שאין כותבין ודאי דלית ליה במעות כלום:

ואינו יכול לדחותו אצל קרקע וכו' אמרינן בגמ' דכתוב' דף צ"ב ראובן שמכר שדה לשמעון באחריות וזקף עליו הדמים במלוה ומת ראובן ואתא ב"ח דראובן וקטריף ליה משמעון ופייסי' בזוזי דינא הוא דקאמרי בני ראובן מטלטלין שביק אבוהון גבך ומטלטלי דיתמי לא משתעבד אמר רבא אי פקח הוא מגבי להו קרקע והדר גבי' מיני' דאמר ר"ן יתומים שגבו קרקע ב"ח חוזר וגובה מהן. והקשו התוס' שם דהא דינא דב"ח בזוזי ואיך יכול לסלקו בקרקע ותי' התוס' הואיל דאיכא פסידא ללוה שעי"כ יפסיד חובו מצי להגבהו קרקע אף דיש לו זוזי. והעתיקו הטור דבמקום פסידא יכול לסלקו בקרקע והב"י תמה עליו בבדק הבית דהא לא נ"מ הך דינא לדידן דתקנו הגאונים לגבות ממטלטלין דיתמי ואם כן אין נ"מ אי מגבהו מעות או קרקע ולכן השמיטו בש"ע. והב"ח בסי' ק"ז דחק ליישב לדעת הטור. ולפי מה שכתוב לקמן בסי' ק"ז בשם שערים דר"א ויתר המחברים בשני ב"ח דאחד יש לו בשטרו מא"ק ואחד לית ליה דיש לזה שיש לו קדימה לגבות משל יתומים דזה גובה מדינא וזה אינו גובה רק מכח תקנה ע"ש מ"ש באריכות ולפ"ז מיירי דהך שמעון שקנה שדה מראובן באחריות לא נכתב בשטרו מטלטלין והקרקע ויש כאן על ראובן ב"ח מאוחר דאיכא בשטרו מטלטלין וקרקע ואם כן אם יפרע שמעון זוזי יבא ב"ח מאוחר ויטרפנו כי יש לו שעבוד של ת רה ולכך פקח להגבות קרקע ושעבודו מוקדם וגובה קרקע ולק"מ וא"ש וכהנה רבי' הנ"מ:

en_segments: If he has money, etc. The Shach in seif katan 1 writes that the same applies to a woman's ketubah: if the heirs possess cash, she may demand it, as he attributes to the Tur, Even HaEzer siman 100, and to a responsum of Maharshal in the name of Rabbi David Kohen. What is obvious to him is very doubtful to me. First, below in siman 107 it is explicit that where heirs possess both movable property and land, a creditor cannot insist on movable property. The Beit Yosef, citing Rabbenu Yonah, writes that the same applies to money and land. If the heirs can therefore turn him from cash to land, why could they not turn him from cash to other movable property, which is superior to land and is deemed better payment? I searched the Tur in Even HaEzer and found no such statement. There is also an error in the citation to the responsum. The source is not Rabbi David Kohen, but the Tashbetz. Indeed, in the relevant responsum it is stated explicitly in the name of Rabbenu Shimon ben Tzemach that if the husband left cash, the widow collects her ketubah, its additional amount, and her dowry from that cash. Yet in Tashbetz, part 3, siman 99, he rules regarding a widow who wished to collect cash from the heirs while they wished to give her land, where the land was property she had brought into the marriage, that because she had originally brought that land she could not demand cash. This implies that had she not brought that land, they would have had to pay her cash, apparently contrary to the authorities cited above. It must therefore be that in the Tashbetz's locale ketubot were customarily written to bind both movable property and land. In that case the heirs' movable property was encumbered by law, not merely by the Geonic enactment described below in siman 107. The reasons offered by the authorities for permitting heirs to turn a creditor from cash or movable property to land then fall away, because those reasons rest on the fact that movable property of heirs was liable only by Geonic enactment while land was liable by Torah law. Where movable property itself was expressly encumbered, the Tashbetz's ruling is coherent: when cash is present, she cannot be turned to land. But in a ketubah that does not contain such a clause, where the law permits the heirs to turn her from cash to land, it follows all the more that they may turn her to movable property, which is considered better payment. Even so, I remain somewhat doubtful. Rabbenu Tam's entire reason that a creditor who lent money receives money when available is that he gave money and should receive money, and even Rabbenu Chaim Kohen disputed that. This rationale applies to a dowry that she actually brought in cash, but not to the basic ketubah, for which she gave no money. On this point, however, I defer to the Tashbetz. It is nevertheless clear that his ruling concerns a place where the ketubah expressly binds movable property and land, as demonstrated above. Where it does not, she has no special right to cash.

And he cannot turn him to land, etc. The Gemara in Ketubot 92 states that Reuven sold a field to Shimon with warranty and converted the purchase price into a loan. Reuven died, Reuven's creditor seized the field from Shimon, and Shimon appeased that creditor with cash. Reuven's heirs could then say that their father left movable property in Shimon's hands, and movable property of heirs is not encumbered. Rava says that if Shimon is clever, he first transfers land to the heirs in payment and then collects it back from them, under Rav Nachman's rule that when heirs collect land, their father's creditor may collect that land from them. Tosafot ask that a creditor's legal payment is cash, so how can Shimon pay the heirs with land when he has cash? They answer that because Shimon would otherwise suffer a loss by losing his claim, he may pay with land despite possessing cash. The Tur accordingly rules that in a case of loss a debtor may turn the creditor to land. The Beit Yosef, in Bedek HaBayit, objects that this rule has no practical application after the Geonic enactment permitting collection from heirs' movable property, and therefore omitted it from the Shulchan Aruch. The Bach in siman 107 labored to defend the Tur. According to what is written below in siman 107 in the name of Shaarei Rav Hai and other authorities, however, where two creditors exist, one whose document expressly binds movable property together with land and one whose document does not, the former has priority against heirs because his claim is effective by law, while the latter collects only by enactment. Accordingly, the case can readily occur where Shimon's warranty document did not bind movable property, while a later creditor of Reuven did have such a clause. If Shimon pays cash, the later creditor will seize it because his lien is legally effective. Shimon is therefore clever to transfer land, against which his earlier lien gives him priority, and then collect it. Thus the Tur's rule remains fully applicable. However. The Rosh rejected Tosafot's answer and explained that the case is different because the debt itself arose from the land. The Baal HaTerumot, Shaar 4, likewise cites the Raavad as explaining that "if he is clever" means that if he lacks cash he need not pursue cash, but may pay with land. Maharam, in the Prague edition of his responsa, explains that Shimon should pay the heirs before they learn that his field was seized, when they will willingly accept land. According to all these explanations, the Bach asks from the end of Ketubot 111, where a rule of reciprocal collection is established in a case involving heirs, and the Gemara asks why one party should not transfer land to the heirs and then collect it back. If a debtor who has money cannot pay land even to avoid a loss, what is the Gemara's question? The Baal HaTerumot already asked this against the Raavad. The resolution appears as follows. The Mishnah there concerns Reuven who lent to Shimon in Nisan until Iyar, and Shimon then lent to Reuven in Iyar. When Reuven later seeks to collect, Shimon argues that Reuven's document must be forged or paid, for had Shimon truly owed him an already matured debt, Reuven would not then have borrowed from Shimon. Admon accepts Shimon's argument, while the opposing view says that each collects from the other. The Gemara establishes the case with heirs: both claims are legally collectible, but one claimant cannot in practice collect because movable property of heirs is not encumbered. The Gemara then asks why land should not be transferred to the heirs. Those authorities can hold that the rule barring payment with land where cash is available applies only when the debtor is known to own the cash. If he says that the money visible in his possession belongs to others, whether deposited by a Jew or a non Jew, it cannot necessarily be taken from him. The Shulchan Aruch, following the Hagahot Maimoniyot, rules that even visible funds may be claimed to belong to others. Although some authorities presume that whatever is in a person's possession is his, many dispute this, as explained above in siman 99. Moreover, where the creditor will be paid in any event and the only issue is whether payment is in cash or land, all should agree that the debtor's claim that the money belongs to others is sufficient, since the alleged true owners can say that the creditor loses nothing, as he is receiving payment from the debtor's land. A relatively weak claim and migo suffice where collection itself is assured. This also resolves the Giddulei Terumah's question on the Baal HaTerumot, who derives from the rule concerning one who attributes his money to a non Jew that where everyone knows he has cash but he claims it belongs to others, beit din compels him to sell land and bring money to his creditor. The Giddulei Terumah asks why this trouble is necessary, since money in one's possession should be presumed his. The Shach answers that the case concerns a violent non Jew whose funds cannot be touched, as the Ritva indeed writes, but the Baal HaTerumot speaks generally and not specifically of a violent person. According to the foregoing, his formulation is correct: since the creditor can be paid from land, the ordinary possession presumption does not justify taking money that the debtor says belongs to others. We may now understand the Gemara. Reuven must be the one who died. If Shimon, the second lender, had died, Shimon's estate would collect from Reuven while Reuven could not collect from them, and that would already amount to Admon's result. Rather, Shimon is alive and Reuven died. Admon says Shimon need not pay, while the other view says that Shimon must pay and Reuven's heirs need not pay him. The Gemara therefore asks why Shimon should lose. He can transfer land to them. If one objects that he has money, he can say it belongs to others. Nor can one say that we are dealing with a wicked man who would lie before beit din and perhaps swear falsely, for he already claims that he owes Reuven nothing. He is believed under oath through a migo: he could have said that the money was not his, in which case he would pay land and then collect his own debt back. Thus the Gemara's question is sound. By contrast, in the earlier case of the clever purchaser, if he actually has cash, his only way to avoid paying it would be to lie to beit din and risk an oath or cherem. There Tosafot's question remains. In practical law, however, Tosafot's ruling is correct: where payment in cash would cause the debtor a loss, he may pay with land. The Rosh's alternative was offered as dialectical explanation rather than a rejection of the law, as is also indicated by his rulings and the Tur. Thus the rule is clear.

he_segments: היו לו. כנ"ל בסי' ק"א ס"ב:
(ליקוט) ה"ל כו'. עתוס' ח' ב' ד"ה מצי כו' (ע"כ):
וי"א דאין. כנ"ל היו לו כו' ועברא"ש:

(ליקוט) אם חפץ כו' וי"א כו'. וראיתו שהרי אפי' בבינונית ששיעבודו עליו יכול לדחותו ואי"ל תן לי משדה פלונית כנ"ל ועתוס' שם ד"ה מצי כו' אבל ס' הראשונה ס"ל אע"ג דבבינונית ובינונית אי"ל בכה"ג יכול לומר וראיה ממ"ש ח' ב' א"ר ראובן שמכר כו' ולא אמרן אלא כו' דא"ל להכי דייקי כו' והקשה הרשב"א בחידושיו שם ה"ד אי לא שייר בינונית ביד שמעון הרי זיבורית שביד לוי שעבודיה עליו ואי דשייר בינונית ל"ל למימר להכי כו' הא אף במכר בינונית בשייר בינונית א"י לגבות ותי' דשאני בינונית ובינונית דיכול לדחותו על בינונית שביד שמעון משא"כ בבינונית וזיבורית שא"י לדחותו לבינונית ולהכי צ"ל להכי דייקי כו' ועתוס' שם ד"ה אבל כו' וע"ל סי' קי"ט ס"א (ע"כ):

(ליקוט) וי"א כו'. וראייתו ממ"ש ח' ב' רצה מזה כו' ודוקא משום שמכר הבינונית ללוי אבל בלא"ה לא גבי מזבורית של שמעון. רא"ש שם ס"ד ואינו מוכרח דעיקר אתא לאשמעינן שי"ל מיד לוי דכל השקלא וטריא שם משום לגבות מלוי ועתוס' שם ד"ה אבל שכ' להיפך (ע"כ):
en_segments: If he had, etc. This follows siman 101, seif 2.

And some say that he cannot, etc. This follows the foregoing rule. Rosh is cited. The first opinion reasons that although a creditor ordinarily cannot demand a specific intermediate-quality field, he may do so when the alternative is inferior land in another's hands. Rashba distinguishes between equal-quality fields and intermediate versus inferior land. The second view relies on Bava Kamma 8b, but that proof is not conclusive. See citation 119.
